Volume 05 · Chapter 02

Demand, duality and welfare

Undergraduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v05-c01

By the endDecompose price responses and measure welfare with correct income concepts.

What income would preserve a standard of living?

Capability: decompose price responses and measure welfare with correct income concepts. Prerequisite: Preferences and consumer choice, especially ordinal utility, local nonsatiation, budget exhaustion and Marshallian demand. The chain rule and Hessians in multivariable calculus, and value-function reasoning in duality and sensitivity, support the derivations.

A household faces a higher food price. Keeping its old basket affordable is one compensation rule; preserving its old welfare while allowing substitution is another. Observed demand changes mix substitution with the loss of purchasing power. We need to separate these mechanisms before using a demand curve to value the price change.

All examples below are original, synthetic consumer models. Quantities are divisible units consumed during one fixed period; prices are dollars per corresponding unit and income is dollars available in that period. A utility number ranks bundles for one consumer. It is neither dollars nor a quantity that can automatically be compared across people.

Two choice problems and four objects

Let x ∈ ℝⁿ+ be a consumption vector, p ≫ 0 a vector of strictly positive prices, m ≥ 0 income and U(x) a utility representation. Use capital U for utility of a bundle and u for a target utility number. The dot product p·x = Σᵢpᵢxᵢ is total expenditure. Define:

  • Marshallian demand: D(p,m) = argmax {U(x): x ≥ 0, p·x ≤ m}. This is a set, called a correspondence; write x(p,m) when the optimizer is unique.
  • Indirect utility: v(p,m) = max {U(x): x ≥ 0, p·x ≤ m}. This is the best utility attainable with a given budget, not a bundle.
  • Expenditure: e(p,u) = min {p·x: x ≥ 0, U(x) ≥ u}. This is the least money needed to reach the specified target.
  • Hicksian demand: H(p,u) = argmin {p·x: x ≥ 0, U(x) ≥ u}. Write h(p,u) for a unique optimizer. Hicksian, or compensated, demand holds utility fixed while the required budget changes with prices.

Our basic duality assumptions are that U is continuous and locally nonsatiated on ℝⁿ+, prices are strictly positive, and targets u are attainable and satisfy u ≥ U(0). Local nonsatiation means every relative neighborhood of any bundle contains a strictly preferred bundle. We do not assume differentiability, strict convexity or uniqueness for the basic identities. Derivative statements below add their own hypotheses.

The budget set is nonempty and compact: 0 ≤ xᵢ ≤ m/pᵢ. Continuity therefore gives a utility maximum. Local nonsatiation makes every maximizing bundle exhaust the budget, since a bundle with slack has a small affordable neighborhood containing a preferred alternative. It also makes v strictly increasing in m: any optimizer at a lower income has slack at a higher income and can be improved.

Expenditure attainment needs a separate argument because the upper contour set {x: U(x) ≥ u} can be unbounded. Choose any feasible bundle a. Minimization may be restricted to its cost sublevel p·x ≤ p·a; this intersection is closed, bounded and nonempty. A minimum therefore exists. At a minimizing bundle b, U(b) = u. If U(b) > u and b ≠ 0, continuity makes (1−ε)b feasible for small ε > 0 at strictly lower cost. If b = 0, the assumed u ≥ U(0) already gives equality. Thus targets below U(0), infeasible targets and zero prices require separate treatment.

The dual identities, including sets of optimal bundles

Under these assumptions,

e(p,v(p,m)) = m,   H(p,v(p,m)) = D(p,m),
v(p,e(p,u)) = u,   D(p,e(p,u)) = H(p,u).

For the first line, a utility-maximizing bundle attains v at cost m. If v could be reached more cheaply, local nonsatiation could improve that cheaper bundle while staying below m, contradicting maximality. Consequently its minimum cost is m. Every expenditure minimizer at target v then belongs to the utility maximizers, and conversely.

For the second line, a minimum-cost bundle reaches u at income e. If another bundle afforded at e gave strictly more than u, continuity would let us shrink it slightly and still reach u at lower cost, a contradiction when e > 0. When e = 0, positive prices leave only the zero bundle and u = U(0). Therefore v(p,e) = u, and the optimizing sets coincide. These arguments also explain why satiation or an inappropriate target can break the stated identities.

Scaling all prices and income by a > 0 leaves D and v unchanged. Scaling just prices multiplies e by a and leaves H unchanged, because the expenditure objective is multiplied by a without changing its feasible set. Expenditure is nondecreasing in each price and in the target; over attainable targets u ≥ U(0) it is strictly increasing in u. To see strictness, equal minimum costs at two distinct targets would make the higher-target optimizer also a lower-target optimizer, contradicting the no-excess-utility result.

Replacing U by any strictly increasing transformation T∘U changes utility labels but leaves upper contour sets and choices unchanged. In particular, eT(p,T(u)) = e(p,u) and vT(p,m) = T(v(p,m)). Dollar welfare measures built with matching target labels therefore survive a change of utility representation.

Price derivatives and envelope conditions

Fix an attainable target u. For any b ∈ H(p,u) and any other positive price vector q, the old bundle b remains feasible. Therefore

e(q,u) ≤ q·b = e(p,u) + (q−p)·b.

This supporting inequality says that allowing reoptimization costs no more than mechanically repricing the old bundle. If e is differentiable in p, use q = p + td with positive and negative small t; the inequality forces ∇pe(p,u)·d = b·d for every direction d. Thus ∂e/∂pᵢ = hᵢ(p,u), known as Shephard's lemma. A dollar-per-unit price change times demanded units gives a dollar expenditure change.

A useful sufficient condition for this differentiability is continuity of U and a unique Hicksian minimizer at the positive price vector under consideration. Here is why. Nearby minimizers are uniformly bounded by the cost of a fixed feasible bundle and a positive lower bound on nearby prices. Any convergent subsequence of these minimizers must be feasible and optimal at the limiting prices, so uniqueness makes all of them converge to h(p,u). The two optimality comparisons give

(q−p)·h(q,u) ≤ e(q,u)−e(p,u) ≤ (q−p)·h(p,u).

Consequently the error after subtracting (q−p)·h(p,u) is at most ‖q−p‖‖h(q,u)−h(p,u)‖ in absolute value, which is o(‖q−p‖). A nearby minimizer can be selected if the nearby set is not unique; the same convergence argument applies to any selection. At ties the supporting inequality still holds, but a single derivative may not exist.

For Roy's identity, suppose v is differentiable in (p,m), e is differentiable in p, and vm > 0 at a positive income m = e(p,u). Differentiate the identity v(p,e(p,u)) = u, holding u fixed:

vpᵢ + vmepᵢ = 0, hence xᵢ(p,m) = −vpᵢ(p,m)/vm(p,m).

The ratio has units (utility per dollar-per-unit)/(utility per dollar), giving units of good i. Strictly increasing indirect utility need not have a strictly positive derivative at every point. The condition vm > 0 must be checked; a flat derivative created by an ordinal transformation can make the ratio 0/0 even when demand is unique.

The same result has an envelope interpretation. On a differentiable interior optimal branch for a continuously differentiable U, the first-order conditions are ∇U(x) = λp, with budget p·x = m. Differentiating the value U(x(p,m)) and the budget gives vm = λ and vpᵢ = −λxᵢ. This derivation assumes that the branch exists and is optimal; first-order equations alone do not establish either fact. With a fixed set of zero quantities, the same argument applies to the active goods. At a change of active set, return to value-function differentiability or one-sided arguments. The constrained-optimization chapter explains the corresponding multiplier conditions.

The official MIT consumer-theory slides provide an independent route through the expenditure problem, Shephard's lemma, Roy's identity and demand duality. Here the elementary attainment and envelope arguments make the restrictions used in our calculations explicit.

Deriving the substitution and income decomposition

At strictly positive prices and positive income, suppose demands are unique and continuously differentiable locally, and e is twice continuously differentiable in prices. Fix a utility target u and write the vector identity x(p,e(p,u)) = h(p,u). Its ith coordinate, differentiated with respect to price pⱼ, gives

∂xᵢ/∂pⱼ + (∂xᵢ/∂m)(∂e/∂pⱼ) = ∂hᵢ/∂pⱼ.

Shephard's lemma and demand duality replace ∂e/∂pⱼ by hⱼ = xⱼ. Evaluating at u = v(p,m) yields the Slutsky equation:

∂xᵢ/∂pⱼ = Sᵢⱼ − xⱼ∂xᵢ/∂m,   Sᵢⱼ = ∂hᵢ/∂pⱼ.

The left side holds nominal income fixed. The substitution term Sᵢⱼ holds utility fixed. To do that after a small price increase dpⱼ requires extra income dm = xⱼdpⱼ to first order; withholding that compensation produces the income term −xⱼ(∂xᵢ/∂m)dpⱼ. All derivatives are evaluated at the same matched price, income and utility. The matrix form is S = Dpx + (Dmx)xᵀ, with row i, column j describing the response of good i to price j.

The sign restrictions follow from optimization. For 0 ≤ t ≤ 1, every feasible bundle a has [tp+(1−t)q]·a ≥ te(p,u)+(1−t)e(q,u). Minimizing the left side proves that e is concave in prices. It is a minimum of linear costs; this concavity does not require convex preferences. Its Hessian S is therefore negative semidefinite: dᵀSd ≤ 0 for every price-change direction d. Twice continuous differentiability makes S symmetric through equality of mixed partials. Hence Sᵢᵢ ≤ 0, but off-diagonal entries can have either sign. Degree-one homogeneity of e makes h degree zero, so differentiating h(ap,u) in a at a = 1 gives Sp = 0. A proportional price change alone does not alter compensated quantities.

Without differentiability, choose b ∈ H(p,u) and c ∈ H(q,u). Cost optimality gives p·b ≤ p·c and q·c ≤ q·b. Adding yields (q−p)·(c−b) ≤ 0. This finite compensated law of demand survives kinks and multiple optima. It does not say that every quantity falls when several prices move.

Locally, a good is normal if ∂xᵢ/∂m > 0, inferior if that derivative is negative, and has no local income effect when it is zero. For an own-price increase, normality reinforces the nonpositive substitution effect. An inferior good has an offsetting income effect. It is Giffen only when ∂xᵢ/∂pᵢ > 0: the positive income term must dominate |Sᵢᵢ|. Inferiority is necessary for Giffen behavior at a smooth point with xᵢ > 0, but it is insufficient. These classifications concern specified price/income regions, not permanent moral or physical properties of goods.

Worked example 1 — Demand identities and a complete Slutsky matrix

Let U(x₁,x₂) = √(x₁x₂). For m > 0 and p₁,p₂ > 0, nonnegative expenditure shares satisfy p₁x₁+p₂x₂ ≤ m. The identity (a−b)² ≥ 0 gives ab ≤ (a+b)²/4. Applying it to a = p₁x₁ and b = p₂x₂ proves that x₁x₂ ≤ m²/(4p₁p₂), with equality at equal spending. Therefore

x₁ = m/(2p₁),   x₂ = m/(2p₂),   v(p,m) = m/(2√(p₁p₂)).

For target u > 0, cost obeys p₁x₁+p₂x₂ ≥ 2√(p₁p₂x₁x₂) ≥ 2u√(p₁p₂). Equality is feasible when x₁x₂ = u² and the spending shares are equal. Thus

e(p,u) = 2u√(p₁p₂),   h₁ = u√(p₂/p₁),   h₂ = u√(p₁/p₂).

These are global optima, not just stationary candidates. At p = (2,8) and m = 96 dollars, x = (24,6), v = 12 and e(p,12) = 96. Differentiating e reproduces h. Roy gives −vp₁/vm = −(−3)/(1/8) = 24 and similarly 6 for good 2.

At this point Dpx = [[−12,0],[0,−3/4]], Dmx = (1/4,1/16)ᵀ, and (Dmx)xᵀ = [[6,3/2],[3/2,3/8]]. Adding produces

S = [[−6,3/2],[3/2,−3/8]].

The own response of good 1 is −12 = −6−24(1/4): half is substitution and half is the lost purchasing power. The zero Marshallian cross response is 0 = 3/2−6(1/4); it conceals a positive compensated cross response. Symmetry holds, Sp = 0, and dᵀSd = −(3/8)(4d₁−d₂)² ≤ 0. Each Sᵢⱼ has units of good i times good j per dollar. These are local derivatives; multiplying them by a large price change does not produce an exact finite response.

Compensating and equivalent variation: specify signs and targets

Keep nominal income m fixed and change prices from p⁰ to p¹. Define u⁰ = v(p⁰,m) and u¹ = v(p¹,m). This chapter uses a positive-loss convention for both measures:

MeasureDefinition in dollarsIndifference condition and question
Compensating variation, CVe(p¹,u⁰) − mv(p¹,m+CV) = u⁰. How much extra income after the change restores initial welfare?
Equivalent variation, EVm − e(p⁰,u¹)v(p⁰,m−EV) = u¹. How much income removed before the change produces the final welfare?

For a welfare loss both numbers are positive; for a gain they are negative; if welfare is unchanged both are zero. Under a gain, −CV is the amount removable after the improvement, whereas −EV is the amount that would have to be added before it. A price increase in goods the consumer never values need not create a strict loss. Other authors define signed welfare gains as positive, reversing both signs. Always state the indifference equations before interpreting an answer.

Using duality, CV = e(p¹,u⁰)−e(p⁰,u⁰), while EV = e(p¹,u¹)−e(p⁰,u¹). If just price i changes and the expenditure function is continuously differentiable along the path, the fundamental theorem of calculus gives

CV = ∫pᵢ⁰pᵢ¹ hᵢ(p,u⁰) dpᵢ,   EV = ∫pᵢ⁰pᵢ¹ hᵢ(p,u¹) dpᵢ.

All other prices stay fixed in these integrals. A piecewise smooth expenditure function can be integrated segment by segment. For simultaneous changes, integrate h(p,u)·dp along a price path at the same fixed target; since this is the differential of e, the endpoints determine the result. With corners or nondifferentiability, expenditure differences remain the primary definitions.

The Marshallian consumer-surplus loss for a single price change is the area LCS = ∫ xᵢ(p,m) dpᵢ with nominal income fixed. It generally differs from both compensated areas. For a small price change all three have the same first-order value xᵢdpᵢ under the smooth assumptions; differences enter at higher order. For a finite change, a large income effect can make the discrepancy material. If the good is normal throughout the relevant income and price range and only its price rises, hᵢ(p,u¹) ≤ xᵢ(p,m) ≤ hᵢ(p,u⁰) along the path, so EV ≤ LCS ≤ CV. The order follows because intermediate attainable utility lies between u¹ and u⁰, and higher utility requires higher expenditure and higher normal-good demand. Inferiority throughout that range reverses the demand and area ordering.

The MIT applications slides connect welfare to expenditure at reference prices and distinguish compensated from Marshallian areas. Their signed-gain definitions have the opposite sign to this chapter's positive-loss convention. The consumer, target, prices and actual income transfer matter more than the abbreviation alone.

Worked example 2 — Exact compensation versus an old basket

Continue the preceding household with m = 96 and U = √(x₁x₂). Raise p₁ from 2 to 8, holding p₂ = 8. Initially x⁰ = (24,6) and u⁰ = 12. Finally x¹ = (6,6) and u¹ = 6. Utility falls by six in this representation, but that number is not a dollar loss.

At new prices, attaining u⁰ costs e((8,8),12) = 192; thus CV = 96 dollars. Giving that transfer produces x = (12,12), utility 12. At old prices, attaining u¹ costs e((2,8),6) = 48; hence EV = 48 dollars. Removing that amount from initial income produces x = (12,3), utility 6. The different reference situations explain the difference between CV and EV.

The fixed-income demand is x₁(p₁,8,96) = 48/p₁, so LCS = 48 ln(8/2) = 48 ln 4 ≈ 66.5421 dollars. Directly integrating h₁ = u√(8/p₁) yields 2u√8(√8−√2) = 8u: 96 at u⁰ = 12 and 48 at u¹ = 6. The area ordering is 48 < 66.5421 < 96.

Repricing the old basket costs 8(24)+8(6) = 240 dollars. A 144-dollar transfer would keep that basket affordable, exceeding CV by 48 because compensation need not prohibit substitution. Indeed the supporting inequality gives CV ≤ (p¹−p⁰)·x⁰ = 144. This upper bound concerns the consumer's old utility, not a general claim that any observed price index overstates every person's cost of living.

When the ordinary area is exact, and when a corner spoils it

A numeraire is a good whose price sets the monetary unit. Normalize its price to one dollar per unit and call its quantity z. A utility representation of the form U(q,z) = f(q)+z is quasilinear in z. If the optimal z remains positive over all relevant uncompensated and compensated paths, the marginal utility of money in this representation is one. For a differentiable strictly concave f, the interior condition f′(q) = p determines q independently of income. Then the same q(p) appears in CV, EV and LCS; the three areas agree exactly. The nonnegative-numeraire restriction can make this fail.

Worked example 3 — Derive the corner before using quasilinearity

Use U(q,z) = 2√q+z, q,z ≥ 0, and budget pq+z ≤ m, with p > 0. In these fixed units the coefficient on √q is calibrated to the numeraire units; rescaling physical quantities requires rescaling that coefficient. Substitution of the exhausted budget gives 2√q+m−pq on 0 ≤ q ≤ m/p. Its derivative for q > 0 is 1/√q−p, positive below q = 1/p² and negative above. Therefore

q(p,m) = min{m/p,1/p²},   z(p,m) = m−pq(p,m),
v(p,m) = 2√(m/p) if m ≤ 1/p;   v(p,m) = m+1/p if m ≥ 1/p.

To derive expenditure for target u ≥ 0, fix q and purchase the minimum z = max{u−2√q,0}. For q ≤ u²/4, cost is pq+u−2√q, minimized at q = 1/p² if that point is in this range. For q ≥ u²/4, cost is pq, minimized at the boundary. Thus

e(p,u) = pu²/4 if 0 ≤ u ≤ 2/p;   e(p,u) = u−1/p if u ≥ 2/p.
At the lower-target branch hq = u²/4, hz = 0; at the upper-target branch hq = 1/p², hz = u−2/p.

The formulas agree at the join u = 2/p. The expenditure function is continuously differentiable there, but its second price derivative changes from 0 to −2/p³; a smooth Slutsky matrix across the join is not justified. A unique choice can coexist with a failure of second differentiability.

Now take m = 5 dollars and p: 1 → 2. Initially (q,z) = (1,4), u⁰ = 6; finally (q,z) = (1/4,9/2), u¹ = 11/2. Both targets exceed 2/p for every p ∈ [1,2], so their compensated paths have positive z. CV = (6−1/2)−5 = 1/2; EV = 5−(11/2−1) = 1/2. Also LCS = ∫₁²p⁻²dp = 1/2 dollar. Expenditure differences verify the area result without assuming it.

At lower income, an observed path can have positive z while a hypothetical EV path reaches z = 0. Check both utility targets and the whole relevant price interval before declaring the three measures equal. Exercise 7 makes this distinction concrete.

From an individual calculation to a policy claim

A dollar welfare measure answers a specified consumer's counterfactual question, conditional on preferences, available goods and the budget constraint. It does not by itself identify preferences from data or estimate a causal price effect. Nor does summing such dollars establish interpersonal utility comparisons. Actual compensation and its funding, producer effects, externalities, access restrictions and distribution require additional analysis. A transfer large enough in total can still leave a particular household worse off.

The model here treats the income m in the price comparison as fixed and externally given. If prices also change labor income, ownership income or taxes, define the new income explicitly and compare e(p¹,u⁰) with that actual new income. Do not silently insert fixed-income CV into a problem with endogenous income. The next market chapters add firm behavior and equilibrium; the individual decomposition remains a useful accounting of mechanisms.

Exercises

  1. For U = √(x₁x₂), p = (3,12) and m = 72 dollars, calculate Marshallian demand and indirect utility. Separately find expenditure and Hicksian demand for target u = 9. Verify the matching dual identity. Then double both prices while holding that target fixed. What changes? Finally replace U by T(U) = (U−6)³: do choices or expenditure for the corresponding target change, and can Roy's ratio be used at the original income?
  2. Reconstruct the argument for expenditure attainment under continuous U, positive prices and an attainable target. Explain why no excess utility follows for u ≥ U(0). Test the necessity of the duality restrictions with the one-good examples (a) U(x) = min{x,2}, p = 3, m = 12 and (b) U(x) = 1+x, p = 3, target u = 0. Calculate the relevant demand sets or values that expose each failure.
  3. For U = √(x₁x₂), p = (4,1), m = 40, derive Dpx, Dmx and S. Check the own- and cross-price Slutsky equations, symmetry, Sp = 0 and negative semidefiniteness by writing dᵀSd as a negative square. Verify Roy's identity at this point. State what is fixed in each derivative.
  4. At a smooth point a good has demand 8 units, income derivative −0.3 units/dollar, and compensated own-price derivative −1.6 units²/dollar. Determine its Marshallian own-price derivative and classification. Repeat with income derivative −0.1. Explain why inferiority alone is insufficient for Giffen behavior. Separately assess the candidate compensated two-good matrix [[−1,2],[2,−1]] under the chapter's smooth utility-maximization assumptions; are negative diagonal entries enough?
  5. Let U(x₁,x₂) = 2x₁+x₂. Derive e(p,u) for u > 0. At p = (6,3) and u = 12, find the entire Hicksian demand set and expenditure. Calculate the left and right derivatives of e with respect to p₁ at the tie, holding p₂ fixed. Choose b = (3,6) at the tie and verify the finite compensated law for q = (8,3) and its unique Hicksian choice. Explain which version of the envelope result remains valid.
  6. For U = √(x₁x₂), m = 60 and p₂ = 1, reduce p₁ from 9 to 4. Compute both utility levels, CV, EV and the Marshallian surplus loss. Give the two resulting income levels that verify the CV/EV indifference equations. Interpret every negative sign. Is the dollar change in the cost of the old basket the exact compensation?
  7. In the quasilinear model of Worked example 3, take m = 1 dollar and p: 1 → 4. Find both chosen bundles and utility levels. Calculate CV, EV and LCS using the piecewise expenditure function. Identify where the final-utility Hicksian path changes branch. Explain why observing q = 1/p² along the fixed-income price path does not suffice to conclude CV = EV.
  8. Two households both have U = √(x₁x₂), with incomes 40 and 120 dollars. Prices change from (1,4) to (4,4). An analyst proposes a 90-dollar grant to each, arguing: “Total payments exceed total CV, so both households are fully compensated and society necessarily benefits.” Calculate each CV and the initial and post-grant utility levels. Evaluate both claims and propose a distribution of the same 180-dollar grant budget that does restore each consumer at least to initial welfare. State what that calculation leaves unresolved.
Complete solutions and interpretation

  1. x = (72/6,72/24) = (12,3), so v = 6. Target u = 9 instead requires e = 2(9)√36 = 108 dollars and h = (18,9/2); its cost is 54+54 = 108 and utility is √81 = 9. Thus x(p,108) = h(p,9) and v(p,108) = 9, while e(p,v(p,72)) = e(p,6) = 72. Mixing target 9 with the income that yields utility 6 would violate the matching needed in the identities.

    At doubled prices e becomes 216 and h remains (18,9/2). Under the strictly increasing cubic transformation, upper contour sets and choices remain the same; the label corresponding to target 9 is 27. Thus eT(p,27) = 108. At original income v = 6, however, T′(6) = 0, so vT,m and both vT,pᵢ equal zero. Roy's derivative ratio is undefined there even though demand is unchanged. Strict ordinal monotonicity does not imply a strictly positive derivative everywhere.

  2. Select a feasible a. Restrict the search to {x ≥ 0: U(x) ≥ u, p·x ≤ p·a}. Continuity makes this set closed, and positive prices bound each coordinate by (p·a)/pᵢ. It is nonempty and compact, so linear cost attains a minimum. A nonzero minimizer with U(x) > u can be shrunk slightly by continuity at lower cost; a zero minimizer must have U(0) = u when u ≥ U(0). This proves the stated attainment and no-excess result without assuming differentiability.

    In (a), D(3,12) = [2,4] and v = 2. Expenditure to reach 2 is 6 with H(3,2) = {2}; hence e(3,v(3,12)) = 6 ≠ 12 and the demand sets are not equal. Satiation permits optimal bundles with slack. In (b), every nonnegative bundle already exceeds the target 0, so e(3,0) = 0, H(3,0) = {0}, but v(3,e(3,0)) = 1 ≠ 0. The target restriction failed, even though U is continuous and locally nonsatiated.

  3. x = (5,20), v = 10. Fixed-income price derivatives are Dpx = [[−5/4,0],[0,−20]], and fixed-price income derivatives are Dmx = (1/8,1/2)ᵀ. Their outer product with x is [[5/8,5/2],[5/2,10]], so S = [[−5/8,5/2],[5/2,−10]]. Own identities are −5/4 = −5/8−5(1/8) and −20 = −10−20(1/2); cross identities are 0 = 5/2−20(1/8) and 0 = 5/2−5(1/2).

    S holds utility fixed. It is symmetric, S(4,1)ᵀ = (0,0)ᵀ and dᵀSd = −(5/8)(d₁−4d₂)² ≤ 0. Finally vm = 1/4, vp₁ = −5/4 and vp₂ = −5. Roy returns (5,20). The expenditure Hessian and the uncompensated demand Jacobian have different entries because their held-fixed arguments differ.

  4. The first Marshallian derivative is −1.6−8(−0.3) = 0.8 units²/dollar. The good is locally inferior and Giffen. With the second income derivative it is −1.6−8(−0.1) = −0.8: still inferior, but not Giffen. The income effect must exceed 1.6 in magnitude to overturn the substitution effect; here that requires ∂x/∂m < −0.2 units/dollar.

    For the proposed matrix and d = (1,1)ᵀ, dᵀSd = 2 > 0, violating negative semidefiniteness. The matrix cannot be the compensated derivative matrix under the stated assumptions. Negative own-price terms alone do not test curvature in every direction; positive cross terms alone are not a violation. The single-good numerical decomposition does not, by itself, certify an entire globally rationalizable demand system.

  5. One dollar spent on good 1 buys 2/p₁ utility units, and on good 2 buys 1/p₂. Minimizing the cost per utility unit gives e(p,u) = u min{p₁/2,p₂}. If p₁/2 < p₂, H = {(u/2,0)}; if p₁/2 > p₂, H = {(0,u)}; at equality H = {(x₁,x₂) ≥ 0: 2x₁+x₂ = u}. At (6,3), target 12 therefore costs 36, and every bundle on that segment minimizes cost.

    Holding p₂ = 3, e = 12 min{p₁/2,3}. Its left derivative at 6 is 6 and its right derivative is 0, so there is no ordinary price derivative. At q = (8,3) the unique c is (0,12). Then (q−p)·(c−b) = (2,0)·(−3,6) = −6 ≤ 0. For any positive r, the chosen b gives e(r,12) ≤ 36+(r−p)·(3,6), since b remains feasible. This supporting inequality and the finite law remain valid; assigning a single gradient h at the tie does not.

  6. u⁰ = 60/(2√9) = 10 and u¹ = 60/(2√4) = 15. CV = 2(10)(2)−60 = −20 dollars; EV = 60−2(15)(3) = −30 dollars. LCS = 30 ln(4/9) ≈ −24.3279 dollars. All three negatives describe welfare gains under our positive-loss convention.

    After the price reduction, removing 20 leaves income 40 and utility 40/(2√4) = 10, restoring initial welfare. Before the reduction, adding 30 gives income 90 and utility 90/(2√9) = 15, reproducing final welfare. Initially x⁰ = (10/3,30). Its new cost is 4(10/3)+30 = 130/3, so the cost change is −50/3 ≈ −16.6667, rather than CV = −20. Reoptimization permits a larger removal while maintaining initial utility: CV ≤ (p¹−p⁰)·x⁰ remains true even for this price decrease.

  7. Initially q = 1, z = 0 and u⁰ = 2. Finally q = 1/16, z = 3/4 and u¹ = 5/4. At new price 4, target 2 uses the upper-target expenditure branch, giving e(4,2) = 7/4; CV = 3/4 dollar. At old price 1, target 5/4 is below 2/p = 2, so e(1,5/4) = (5/4)²/4 = 25/64 and EV = 39/64 = 0.609375 dollar.

    For m = 1 and p ∈ [1,4], q = 1/p², including the boundary at p = 1. Thus LCS = 1−1/4 = 3/4 dollar, equal to CV but greater than EV. The final-utility Hicksian branch changes when 5/4 = 2/p, at p = 8/5. From 1 to 8/5 it has q = 25/64 and z = 0; from 8/5 to 4 it has q = 1/p². Its integral is (25/64)(3/5)+(5/8−1/4) = 15/64+24/64 = 39/64. Absence of a local income effect along the observed path does not establish absence of income effects along the hypothetical compensation path.

  8. At initial prices v = m/4 and at final prices v = m/8. Restoring initial utility at final prices needs income 2m, so each CV equals its original income: 40 and 120 dollars, totaling 160. Initial utilities are 10 and 30. With 90-dollar grants, incomes become 130 and 210; final utilities are 65/4 = 16.25 and 105/4 = 26.25. The poorer household is more than compensated, but the richer one remains worse off. Total payments of 180 do not prove that their allocation restores both.

    Grants of 40 and 140 use the same 180: final utilities are 80/8 = 10 and 260/8 = 32.5, so both consumers weakly gain relative to their initial positions. This establishes only their model-based consumer comparison conditional on the grants. Financing costs, effects on whoever pays, producers, externalities, observed preference evidence and distributional judgments remain unresolved. The utility numbers themselves cannot be summed as interpersonal welfare without a further ethical and measurement framework.

Teach-back and retention

Teach-back: explain to a colleague why Hicksian demand can be useful even when actual purchases are Marshallian. Derive Slutsky from one composed function, identify every held-fixed variable, and explain why a normal good's own-price response cannot be positive under the smooth assumptions. Then state CV and EV using their indifference equations before drawing either area.

Delayed check: without reopening the examples, use U = √(x₁x₂), m = 24 and prices (1,4) → (4,4). Find both bundles, CV, EV and LCS. State one condition needed for each derivative identity and one reason an observed quasilinear price path can give a misleading claim about EV.

Delayed-check answer

Bundles are (12,3) and (3,3), utilities 6 and 3. CV = 48−24 = 24; EV = 24−12 = 12; LCS = 12 ln 4 ≈ 16.6355 dollars. Shephard requires the relevant price derivative (uniqueness plus continuity and positive prices supplies a sufficient condition); Roy additionally needs nonzero positive vm; the smooth Slutsky derivation needs differentiable matched demand functions. A final-utility compensated path can hit the zero-numeraire boundary even when the observed fixed-income path has no income effect.

Further study and limits

The two cited MIT slide sets are primary course-method sources for the precise topics linked above, not endorsements of this chapter. Our examples, proofs and exercises were independently constructed. This chapter proves the finite-dimensional identities and smooth decompositions it uses; it does not supply the general theory of nonsmooth envelopes, demand integrability or welfare aggregation. Volume 13 develops the planned graduate extensions.

Next, Production, costs and firm choice applies a related minimum-expenditure logic to obtaining output from inputs. The objects, constraints and economic interpretation change even when the mathematics looks familiar.

Sources and further study

  • Alexander Wolitzky, MIT 14.121: Lectures 3–4, Consumer Theory (Fall 2015) — Primary course-method reference for indirect utility, budget multipliers and Roy's identity, expenditure/Hicksian demand, price concavity, Shephard's lemma, dual identities and Slutsky restrictions. Chapter independently supplies its own finite-dimensional proofs, explicit target and positive-derivative restrictions, and numerical cases. Graduate V13-C02 adds full original compact-optimizer envelope/directional proofs, regular Slutsky restrictions and a constructive homothetic duality class.
  • Alexander Wolitzky, MIT 14.121: Lecture 5, Applications of Consumer Theory (Fall 2015) — Primary method reference for expenditure-based money metrics, reference-price choices, CV/EV and compensated versus Marshallian areas. The chapter explicitly defines losses as positive, reversing the source's signed-gain definitions; no historical price-index estimates are imported.
